comments.author: @Proserpira
comments.text:
The video at 7:30 is interesting. It's not at all uncommon in Switzerland, and it's even considered a good thing to be asked to come in and do a "stage", which I think translates to internship?, because that means the job is interested and wants to see how you work to make sure you're suited to the company and know what you're doing or are willing and able to learn.
Then, if hired, there's a 3 month (paid) trial period before you become a full employee. All this counts as proper work experience and should be put on your CV.

For the experience vs schooling, Switzerland's method is making absolutely every possible career an apprenticeship. The majority are what we call dual apprenticeships, where you go to school for both career-specific and high-school level education (most apprenticeships can be started at 15, 18 for most entry-level medical stuff. Also most Swiss people do apprenticeships and never go to high-school) and you have two to three days where you work in your career field.

Apprenticeships are paid for by employers, so you don't go into debt for it. You also receive an apprentice salary.

So you not only have specialised education, but also 3 to 4 years of work experience by the time you enter the job market. Switzerland also has laws that force companies to prioritise the unemployed, as all job offers have to be showcased for a week on a job listing website that only people on unemployment have access to before being allowed to the public.
